speaker: Lisa Blatt
title: Arguing In Front of SCOTUS | Interview: Lisa Blatt
question: In U.S. federal litigation, why has strategic forum shopping become so concentrated in challenges to presidential executive orders?
guest: I think it used to be, when I was growing up, to become a judge, you moved to the middle. Being a moderate got you appointed, and now being a moderate makes you a loser. So you just aren't getting anywhere unless you have either a very woke resume or a very solid, reliably right resume. That's just how you become a judge. It doesn't mean there aren't brilliant judges who fit that, but you're just getting extreme. The forum shopping is just so obvious. You're looking at the Fifth, the First, and the Ninth—a little bit of the Fourth—and those are where all the action is out of executive orders, and it doesn't matter which administration. In terms of forum shopping, I don't really necessarily like that word. Of course I would advise clients to file where they can when they have universal venue. You should.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Forum shopping concentrates in executive-order challenges because the payoff from choosing the right judge is uniquely large and the rules make choosing easy.

On the payoff side, an executive order applies nationwide, so a single district judge who grants broad relief can halt a president's policy everywhere. That makes one favorable ruling worth far more than in ordinary litigation, where a win binds only the parties.

On the ease side, venue rules for suits against the federal government are permissive: plaintiffs can generally sue wherever any plaintiff resides. States, advocacy groups, and trade associations can therefore file almost anywhere, picking circuits with sympathetic appellate benches, and in some places single-judge divisions that virtually guarantee a particular judge. Both parties do this: conservative challengers favored Texas divisions under Biden, while liberal challengers favor districts in Massachusetts, Maryland, Washington, and California under Trump.

Underlying drivers include congressional gridlock, which pushes policymaking into executive orders, and a judiciary whose rulings are increasingly predictable by appointing party.

The Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA curtailed universal injunctions, but class actions, state-plaintiff suits, and APA vacatur preserve much of the incentive.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Strategic forum shopping concentrates around presidential executive orders because unilateral policymaking, permissive venue rules, and sweeping judicial remedies uniquely converge in these disputes. Amid congressional gridlock, presidents increasingly use executive orders to enact immediate national policies, prompting state attorneys general and advocacy groups to deploy litigation as rapid political opposition. Unlike statutes that channel certain regulatory challenges into a designated court like the D.C. Circuit, general federal venue law (28 U.S.C. § 1391(e)) allows suits against federal officials wherever any plaintiff resides. Multistate coalitions and national organizations can therefore select favorable appellate circuits and even single-judge district divisions, virtually guaranteeing a sympathetic judge. Crucially, the remedial stakes create asymmetric incentives: for years, winning just one universal preliminary injunction halted an order nationwide, while losses elsewhere did not bind other challengers. Even after the Supreme Court curtailed universal injunctions in *Trump v. CASA, Inc.* (2025), plaintiffs still target receptive forums to secure nationwide class certifications, Administrative Procedure Act vacatur of implementing agency actions, or broad party-based relief.

noweb.answer: Strategic forum shopping clusters around executive orders because permissive venue rules, local case-assignment practices, and broad remedies combine with an absence of statutory venue channeling. Unlike regulatory statutes that route review exclusively to a single court like the D.C. Circuit, challenges to executive orders typically proceed under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(e), allowing suits against federal officials wherever any plaintiff resides. State attorneys general and national advocacy groups can thus file in almost any district—and, in single-judge divisions, effectively select both the trial judge and the appellate circuit. Because executive orders reshape national policy immediately without Congress, challengers seek sweeping preliminary relief—through broad injunctions, Administrative Procedure Act vacatur of implementing directives, or nationwide class actions—allowing one judge to stall a presidential initiative across the country. That creates a powerful asymmetry: the administration must win everywhere to enforce its policy, whereas opponents need win only once. Amid congressional gridlock and heavy presidential reliance on unilateral action, handpicking sympathetic forums gives litigants rapid, high-reward veto power over national policy.

Forum shopping concentrates in executive-order challenges because several features of these cases line up. Executive orders apply nationwide, so nearly any plaintiff, including a state, trade group, or advocacy organization, can claim injury almost anywhere. The federal venue statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1391(e), lets suits against the government be filed wherever a plaintiff resides, so challengers can pick their courthouse. Many districts have single-judge divisions, so filers often know in advance which judge will hear the case. Federal judges and circuits also differ in ideology. Conservative challengers have favored Texas courts in the Fifth Circuit, while progressive challengers have favored courts in the Ninth and First Circuits and in Maryland.

The payoff has been large. Until 2025, one district judge could issue a universal injunction that froze a presidential policy across the whole country. That made winning in a chosen court worth far more than in ordinary litigation. These disputes are also politically polarized and urgent, so both parties have used them aggressively whenever the presidency changes hands.

In Trump v. CASA (2025), the Supreme Court restricted universal injunctions. Challengers have since moved toward class actions, vacatur of rules under the Administrative Procedure Act, and suits brought by states, so the incentive to choose a favorable court remains.

noweb.answer: Strategic forum shopping concentrates heavily in challenges to presidential executive orders because broad federal venue rules intersect with high-stakes nationwide remedies. Under federal venue statutes, plaintiffs suing the federal government can generally file wherever a plaintiff resides, allowing state attorneys general, national advocacy groups, or plaintiffs recruited from specific jurisdictions to sue almost anywhere in the country. Because executive orders often enact polarizing national policies with immediate effect, and appellate review can take months or years, challengers have an overwhelming incentive to choose the forum most likely to deliver a swift, far-reaching block.

noweb.answer:
Challenges to executive orders combine nationwide stakes with substantial choice over where to sue. When an order affects people or institutions across the country, eligible challengers can often file in several districts. Coalitions of state attorneys general and advocacy groups can coordinate who brings the case and where, favoring a circuit with helpful precedent or a division where the judge assignment is predictable.

Timing magnifies that advantage. A single district judge can temporarily block an order’s implementation before it takes effect or before an appellate court weighs in. Historically, nationwide injunctions let challengers turn one favorable ruling into a halt across the country. The Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in *Trump v. CASA* limited injunctions that reach beyond what is necessary to give the plaintiffs complete relief. Forum choice still matters because the first ruling can determine whether a major policy takes effect for the challengers while the case proceeds.

points.why: The response does not discuss how judicial appointment incentives shifted from favoring moderates to rewarding reliable ideological credentials.
The response describes how challengers choose favorable courts without claiming that challengers from both parties repeatedly target the same few circuits across administrations.
The response explains how broad venue choice lets challengers select favorable courts but does not say that lawyers should choose the strongest permissible forum for their clients.

Challenges to executive orders combine a wide choice of filing locations with an unusually large payoff for winning the first ruling. A nationwide policy can injure parties in many states, and federal venue rules often let an injured plaintiff sue federal officials where the plaintiff resides. A coalition of state attorneys general can therefore choose among several proper districts, taking into account the likely judge and the circuit that would hear an appeal.

Timing makes that choice valuable. A preliminary injunction can shape whether a presidential initiative takes effect during the months or years that appeals take. Historically, a single district judge could halt implementation nationwide, making the initial forum especially consequential. The Supreme Court narrowed that incentive in *Trump v. CASA* (2025) by limiting injunctions to the relief needed to remedy the plaintiffs’ injuries. Forum choice still matters because relief for a multistate coalition or a certified nationwide class can have broad practical effects.
